title: The neutral person
hookLine: the cashier, the neighbor, someone you barely notice

cards: The last person who handed you a coffee: what did they look like? What color was their hair? It's surprisingly hard to say.
Plenty of the people you pass in a day are basically furniture. The bus driver. The person two desks over.
The neighbor whose name you never caught. You don't dislike them. You just don't see them.
Today's step in metta is exactly those people. Not the ones you love, not the ones who annoy you. The ones in the middle, who have somehow become invisible.

teach.b: In the Visuddhimagga's order, after yourself, a benefactor and a dear friend, comes the neutral person: someone you neither like nor dislike. This step is harder than it sounds. With a friend, warmth is already there.

With a neutral person, there's nothing to start from. So you build the wish on something true: this person wants to be happy, exactly as much as you do. They woke up this morning with their own worries.

teach.h: THEY WANT TO BE HAPPY TOO.
teach.b: They have someone they love, something they're afraid of, a song they know every word to. They have a whole life, and you're seeing about four seconds of it.
An old teaching in the Pali texts makes the same point from a longer angle.

teach.h: NO STRANGERS IN A LONG ROUND.
teach.b: The Buddha says the round of rebirth is so long that it's hard to find a being who hasn't, at some point, been your mother, your father, your brother, your sister, your child.
Some Buddhists take that literally, and some hear it as a picture. Either way, the stranger stops being a stranger.
The manual also has a quiet method for this stage: move everyone one step closer. Hold the dear friend the way you held the benefactor, then the neutral person the way you held the dear friend.
The stranger gets a seat that was already warm.
That's the hope of this step: the cashier starts to look like a person again. You remember a name. You look up.
Metta, working quietly, in the least dramatic place in your day.

how: In the traditional order of metta practice, Buddhists extend the wishes to a neutral person, someone they neither like nor dislike, after themselves, a benefactor and a dear friend.

o: a close friend you see every single day
someone who has deeply wronged you
someone you neither like nor dislike

games.q: the steps so far — tap the pairs.

s: the neutral person is easier than the dear friend
there's no warmth to start from, so you build the wish on what's true: they want to be happy too.
the manual asks you to hold the neutral person as you held the dear friend
everyone moves one step closer, so the stranger gets a seat that's already warm.
the Pali texts say it's hard to find a being who hasn't been your mother
the round of rebirth is that long, so the stranger stops being a stranger.

games.q: you're sending metta to a stranger and it feels like nothing. what does the old manual suggest?
o: hold the stranger the way you held your dear friend.
games.why: the Visuddhimagga moves everyone one step closer: the neutral person is held as the dear friend was.

practice: Bring to mind someone you saw recently but don't really know, a cashier, a driver, a neighbor; picture what you can, even if the face is blurry, and remind yourself: they want to be happy, just like me.

Then offer the phrases slowly: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. If it feels thin, let this person sit where your friend sat yesterday, and offer the same wish.

wordCard.voice: Majjhatta. Someone you neither like nor dislike: the fourth step of metta, and the easiest to forget.

orig.note: Pali: standing in the middle, neutral; the manual's word for the neutral person.

carryVoice: Your line: they have a whole life. And they want to be happy, just like you. Until tomorrow.
